title: Cell Structure & Membranes
description: Organelle jobs, endosymbiosis evidence, the cytoskeleton, the fluid mosaic membrane, tonicity, passive vs active transport, the Na⁺/K⁺ pump and junctions.

cards.title: In a prokaryotic cell, what is the region called where the DNA is concentrated without any membrane around it?
cards.body:
The **nucleoid**.

Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) have no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotes enclose their DNA in a nucleus bounded by the nuclear envelope, a double membrane perforated by pores.

Key idea: "prokaryote" means no nucleus, not "no DNA".
cards.searchQuery: prokaryote nucleoid region DNA no membrane

cards.title: Which dense, non-membrane-bound region inside the nucleus makes rRNA and assembles ribosomal subunits?
cards.body:
The **nucleolus**.

rRNA made there is combined with proteins imported from the cytoplasm into large and small subunits, which exit through nuclear pores.

Watch out: the two subunits join into a working ribosome only in the cytoplasm, not in the nucleus.
cards.searchQuery: nucleolus rRNA ribosomal subunit assembly

cards.title: Proteins headed for mitochondria, chloroplasts or the nucleus: are they made on free ribosomes or on ER-bound ribosomes?
cards.body:
**Free ribosomes** in the cytosol.

Free ribosomes make cytosolic proteins and proteins imported later into mitochondria, chloroplasts and the nucleus. (Mitochondria and chloroplasts also make a few proteins on their own ribosomes.)

ER-bound ribosomes make secreted proteins (e.g., insulin), membrane proteins, and proteins for the ER, Golgi and lysosomes.

Key idea: the ribosomes are identical; a **signal peptide** on the new protein sends its ribosome to the ER.
cards.searchQuery: free ribosomes versus bound ribosomes protein destination

cards.title: Which organelle makes lipids such as steroid hormones, detoxifies drugs in liver cells, and stores $\ce{Ca^2+}$ in muscle cells?
cards.body:
**Smooth ER** (no ribosomes).

Drugs such as barbiturates and alcohol make liver cells build more smooth ER, which raises drug tolerance.

In muscle it is called the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and its release of $\ce{Ca^2+}$ triggers contraction.

Watch out: rough ER, studded with ribosomes, makes secretory and membrane proteins instead.
cards.searchQuery: smooth ER functions lipid synthesis detoxification calcium storage

cards.title: Which face of the Golgi apparatus receives the transport vesicles arriving from the ER?
cards.body:
The **cis face** (the receiving side, near the ER).

Products are modified as they pass through the cisternae (e.g., glycoprotein carbohydrates trimmed and altered, phosphate ID tags added). They are then sorted into vesicles that leave from the **trans face**, the shipping side.

Mnemonic: cis = "come in"; trans = "transport out".
cards.searchQuery: Golgi apparatus cis face receiving side

cards.title: In an animal cell, which membrane-bound sac of hydrolytic enzymes digests engulfed food and recycles worn-out organelles?
cards.body:
The **lysosome**.

Its enzymes work best at $\mathrm{pH} \approx 5$, kept acidic by $\ce{H+}$ pumps in its membrane. Enzymes that leak out do little at the cytosol's near-neutral pH ($\approx 7.2$). Recycling organelles is called autophagy.

Example: in Tay-Sachs disease a lipid-digesting lysosomal enzyme is missing, so lipids build up in brain cells.
cards.searchQuery: lysosome hydrolytic enzymes digestion autophagy

cards.title: Which organelle transfers hydrogen from substrates to $\ce{O2}$, producing $\ce{H2O2}$ that its own enzyme then converts to water?
cards.body:
The **peroxisome**.

These reactions break fatty acids into smaller molecules that mitochondria burn as fuel and, in liver cells, detoxify alcohol.

The enzyme **catalase** breaks down the toxic $\ce{H2O2}$: $\ce{2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2}$.

Example: glyoxysomes, specialized peroxisomes in fat-storing seeds, help convert fatty acids to sugar.
cards.searchQuery: peroxisome catalase hydrogen peroxide function

cards.title: Give three lines of evidence that mitochondria and chloroplasts evolved from engulfed prokaryotes.
cards.body:
Any three of the five below.

- A **double membrane**
- Their own circular DNA without histones, like a bacterial chromosome
- Their own ribosomes, which resemble bacterial ribosomes (including antibiotic sensitivity)
- Division by a process like binary fission
- Inner-membrane enzymes and transport systems like those of prokaryotes

Key idea: mitochondria came from an alphaproteobacterium, chloroplasts from a cyanobacterium.
cards.searchQuery: endosymbiont theory evidence mitochondria chloroplasts

cards.title: Which cytoskeletal fibers resist compression, form the mitotic spindle, and make up the core of cilia and flagella?
cards.body:
**Microtubules**: hollow tubes of tubulin dimers, $\approx 25\,\mathrm{nm}$ wide, the thickest fibers.

In animal cells they grow out from the centrosome, and motor proteins carry vesicles along them.

Example: motile cilia and flagella have a $9 + 2$ pattern (nine doublets around two single microtubules), bent by dynein motors.
cards.searchQuery: microtubules tubulin spindle cilia flagella cytoskeleton

cards.title: Which cytoskeletal fibers form the animal cleavage furrow and the core of microvilli, and work with myosin to contract muscle?
cards.body:
**Microfilaments** (actin filaments), $\approx 7\,\mathrm{nm}$ wide, the thinnest fibers.

They bear tension and power amoeboid movement and cytoplasmic streaming.

Watch out: don't confuse them with **intermediate filaments** ($8\text{–}12\,\mathrm{nm}$; e.g., keratins, nuclear lamins), the most permanent fibers, which anchor the nucleus and other organelles in place.
cards.searchQuery: microfilaments actin filaments cytoskeleton function

cards.title: In the fluid mosaic model of a cell membrane, what is 'fluid' and what makes up the 'mosaic'?
cards.body:
**Fluid**: phospholipids (and many proteins) drift sideways within the bilayer. **Mosaic**: many different proteins embedded in or attached to the bilayer.

Flip-flopping of lipids across the bilayer is rare.

Why: unsaturated, kinked fatty acid tails keep membranes fluid in the cold; in animal cells, cholesterol buffers fluidity against temperature changes.
cards.searchQuery: fluid mosaic model membrane phospholipids proteins

cards.title: What happens to an animal cell and to a plant cell placed in a hypotonic solution? In a hypertonic one?
cards.body:
**Hypotonic** (water moves in): the animal cell swells and may lyse; the plant cell becomes turgid, its healthy state, as the wall pushes back.

**Hypertonic** (water moves out): the animal cell shrivels; the plant cell plasmolyzes as its membrane pulls away from the wall.

Key idea: in isotonic solution the animal cell is normal but the plant cell is flaccid (limp).
cards.searchQuery: hypotonic hypertonic animal cell plant cell lysis plasmolysis

cards.title: Glucose enters a red blood cell down its concentration gradient via a carrier protein, using no ATP. What kind of transport is this?
cards.body:
**Facilitated diffusion**, a form of passive transport.

Using a transport protein doesn't make it active: the energy comes from the gradient itself.

Active transport moves solutes against their gradient and needs energy, from ATP or from another solute's gradient (cotransport).
cards.searchQuery: facilitated diffusion passive transport carrier protein glucose

cards.title: For each ATP it uses, how many $\ce{Na+}$ and $\ce{K+}$ ions does the sodium-potassium pump move, and in which directions?
cards.body:
$\ce{3 Na+}$ out and $\ce{2 K+}$ in, both against their concentration gradients (active transport).

ATP phosphorylates the pump, changing its shape.

Why: each cycle exports one net positive charge, so it is an **electrogenic** pump that adds to the negative charge inside the cell.
cards.searchQuery: sodium potassium pump 3 Na out 2 K in ATP

cards.title: Cells take in LDL particles bound to specific proteins clustered in coated pits, which pinch inward. What type of endocytosis is this?
cards.body:
**Receptor-mediated endocytosis**.

The coated pit forms a coated vesicle carrying the LDL inside. Other endocytosis: phagocytosis (cell eating) and pinocytosis (cell drinking). Exocytosis does the reverse, secreting vesicle contents.

Example: in familial hypercholesterolemia, defective or missing LDL receptors leave LDL in the blood, causing early atherosclerosis.
cards.searchQuery: receptor-mediated endocytosis LDL coated pit

cards.title: Which animal cell junctions are protein-lined pores letting ions and small molecules pass straight between cells, as in heart muscle?
cards.body:
**Gap junctions**.

Plant cells use plasmodesmata, channels through their cell walls.

Other animal junctions: **tight junctions** press membranes together into a seal that blocks leakage (e.g., between skin cells); **desmosomes** are rivets, anchored by intermediate filaments, that fasten cells into strong sheets.
cards.searchQuery: gap junctions animal cell communication

cards.title: State the three tenets of cell theory.
cards.body:
1. All living organisms are made of one or more cells.
2. The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in organisms.
3. All cells come from preexisting cells.

The third tenet rules out spontaneous generation of cells today.

Key idea: viruses are not cells, which is one reason they are usually not counted as living.
cards.searchQuery: cell theory three tenets

cards.title: As a cell grows larger while keeping its shape, what happens to its surface-area-to-volume ratio?
cards.body:
It **decreases**.

Surface area scales with length squared, but volume scales with length cubed.

Example: a cube of side $1\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ has $\mathrm{SA}/V = 6/1 = 6$. Doubling the side gives $24/8 = 3$.

Why: a small ratio limits how fast a cell can exchange nutrients and wastes across its membrane, so large cells are flattened, elongated or folded.
cards.searchQuery: surface area to volume ratio cell size decreases

cards.title: What is the Svedberg value of a whole bacterial (prokaryotic) ribosome?
cards.body:
**70S**.

It has a 50S large subunit and a 30S small subunit. Eukaryotic cytosolic ribosomes are **80S** (60S + 40S).

Watch out: S values are sedimentation rates, not masses, so they do not add up ($50 + 30 \neq 70$).

Tip: the difference between 70S and 80S ribosomes is why some antibiotics block bacterial protein synthesis without harming host cells.
cards.searchQuery: prokaryotic ribosome 70S subunits 50S 30S

cards.title: Which polymer of cross-linked sugars and short peptides makes up the bacterial cell wall?
cards.body:
**Peptidoglycan**.

It forms a mesh around the cell that resists osmotic bursting. Archaeal walls lack it.

Example: penicillin blocks the cross-linking of peptidoglycan, so growing bacteria weaken and lyse.
cards.searchQuery: peptidoglycan bacterial cell wall

cards.title: How do the cell walls of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria differ, and how does each look after Gram staining?
cards.body:
**Gram-positive**: a thick peptidoglycan layer that retains crystal violet, so cells look purple.

**Gram-negative**: a thin peptidoglycan layer under an outer membrane. The stain washes out and cells take up the counterstain, looking pink or red.

Why: the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria makes them harder for many antibiotics to penetrate.
cards.searchQuery: Gram positive Gram negative cell wall peptidoglycan outer membrane

cards.title: How does the rotating bacterial flagellum differ from a eukaryotic flagellum?
cards.body:
The bacterial flagellum is a rigid, helical filament of **flagellin** that **rotates** like a propeller, driven by a proton gradient across the plasma membrane.

A eukaryotic flagellum is a membrane-enclosed $9+2$ microtubule structure that bends in a wave, powered by ATP-driven dynein.

Key idea: the two are not homologous; they evolved separately.
cards.searchQuery: bacterial flagellum versus eukaryotic flagellum rotation flagellin

cards.title: Which hairlike bacterial surface appendage forms a bridge for transferring DNA from one cell to another during conjugation?
cards.body:
The **sex pilus**.

Other pili, often called fimbriae, are shorter and help bacteria attach to surfaces and host tissue.

Example: the F pilus lets an F⁺ donor cell link to a recipient and pass over a copy of plasmid DNA.
cards.searchQuery: sex pilus bacterial conjugation DNA transfer

cards.title: What sticky polysaccharide layer outside the cell wall helps some bacteria stick to surfaces and evade phagocytosis?
cards.body:
The **capsule**.

It sits outside the cell wall and is often a polysaccharide (sometimes protein).

Example: encapsulated strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae resist engulfment by white blood cells and are more virulent than unencapsulated ones.
cards.searchQuery: bacterial capsule polysaccharide evade phagocytosis

cards.title: About what is the resolution limit of a light microscope, in nanometers (nm)?
cards.body:
About **200 nm** ($0.2\,\mu\mathrm{m}$).

Resolution is the smallest distance at which two points still look separate. It is limited by the wavelength of visible light, so no lens can fix it.

Example: mitochondria ($\approx 1\,\mu\mathrm{m}$) are visible, but ribosomes ($\approx 25\,\mathrm{nm}$) are not.

Watch out: resolution is not magnification; magnifying beyond the limit only blurs more.
cards.searchQuery: light microscope resolution limit 200 nm

cards.title: Which type of electron microscope scans a beam over a specimen to produce a 3-D-looking image of its surface?
cards.body:
The **scanning electron microscope (SEM)**.

A **transmission electron microscope (TEM)** instead passes electrons through a very thin section to show internal structure such as organelles.

Tip: S for surface, T for through.
cards.searchQuery: scanning electron microscope SEM surface 3D image

cards.title: When a cell homogenate is spun by differential centrifugation, which structures pellet first at the lowest speed?
cards.body:
**Nuclei** (along with unbroken cells and large debris).

The supernatant is respun at higher speeds, pelleting successively smaller structures: mitochondria and chloroplasts, then microsomes (ER fragments), then ribosomes.

Why: larger, denser particles sediment faster, so each speed pulls down a different fraction.
cards.searchQuery: differential centrifugation cell fractionation nuclei pellet first

cards.title: The outer membrane of the nuclear envelope is continuous with which organelle?
cards.body:
The **endoplasmic reticulum** (the rough ER in particular).

The envelope is two lipid bilayers, and the space between them is continuous with the ER lumen.

Key idea: the nuclear envelope is part of the endomembrane system, which also includes the ER, Golgi, lysosomes and vacuoles.
cards.searchQuery: nuclear envelope outer membrane continuous with ER

cards.title: What protein-lined channel structure regulates which molecules enter and leave the nucleus?
cards.body:
The **nuclear pore complex**.

Small molecules diffuse through. Large proteins and RNAs need transport signals: imported proteins carry a **nuclear localization signal**, while mRNA and ribosomal subunits are exported.

Example: transcription factors made in the cytoplasm are imported through nuclear pores to switch on genes.
cards.searchQuery: nuclear pore complex nuclear transport nucleus

cards.title: What mesh of intermediate filaments lining the inner face of the nuclear envelope helps maintain nuclear shape?
cards.body:
The **nuclear lamina**, made of lamin proteins.

It stiffens the nucleus and anchors chromatin and the envelope in place. Lamins are intermediate filaments, the only cytoskeleton-type fibers inside the nucleus.

Why: the lamina breaks down in prophase, when phosphorylated lamins let the envelope fragment, and re-forms in telophase.
cards.searchQuery: nuclear lamina lamins intermediate filaments

cards.title: What is the name for the complex of DNA and proteins that is loosely spread out in the nucleus of a nondividing cell?
cards.body:
**Chromatin**.

It is DNA wrapped around histone proteins. Before cell division it condenses into the compact, visible structures called chromosomes.

Key idea: chromatin and chromosomes are the same material in different states of packing.
cards.searchQuery: chromatin DNA histones interphase nucleus

cards.title: Which RNA-protein complex binds a signal peptide as it emerges from a ribosome and guides the ribosome to the rough ER?
cards.body:
The **signal recognition particle (SRP)**.

After the ribosome docks at a translocation channel in the ER membrane, the growing polypeptide is threaded into the ER lumen as it is made.

Example: insulin carries an ER signal peptide, so its ribosome ends up on the rough ER.
cards.searchQuery: signal recognition particle SRP signal peptide ER

cards.title: What carbohydrate modification begins in the lumen of the rough ER, turning many proteins into glycoproteins?
cards.body:
**Glycosylation**: sugar chains are attached to proteins.

Chaperones in the ER lumen also help proteins fold. Correctly folded proteins are packaged into transport vesicles bound for the Golgi.

Watch out: misfolded proteins are held back in the ER and tagged for degradation.
cards.searchQuery: rough ER glycosylation glycoprotein folding chaperones

cards.title: Which organelle is a stack of flattened sacs that modifies, sorts and packages proteins and lipids, and in plants makes pectin and other wall polysaccharides?
cards.body:
The **Golgi apparatus**.

Its cisternae are chemically distinct: enzymes in each stage perform different modifications, and products leave in vesicles from the trans face.

Example: the Golgi adds the phosphate tag that directs enzymes to lysosomes.
cards.searchQuery: Golgi apparatus modify sort package proteins pectin

cards.title: Trace the path of a secreted protein, such as insulin, from synthesis to release.
cards.body:
Rough ER → transport vesicle → cis Golgi → trans Golgi → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane (exocytosis).

Vesicles bud from one compartment and fuse with the next, so the protein never crosses a membrane after entering the ER lumen.

Watch out: the nucleus is not on the path; the mRNA leaves it, but the protein does not.
cards.searchQuery: secretory pathway rough ER Golgi vesicle exocytosis

cards.title: What is the membrane enclosing the central vacuole of a plant cell called?
cards.body:
The **tonoplast**.

The central vacuole stores water, ions, sugars, pigments and waste, and its pressure on the cytoplasm helps keep the cell turgid.

Example: anthocyanins stored in vacuoles color many flower petals.
cards.searchQuery: tonoplast central vacuole plant cell

cards.title: Which organelle of freshwater protists such as Paramecium pumps excess water out of the cell?
cards.body:
The **contractile vacuole**.

Water continually enters by osmosis because the cell is hypertonic to its pond-water surroundings.

Key idea: without it the cell would swell and burst; the cell wall prevents this in plants and bacteria.
cards.searchQuery: contractile vacuole freshwater protist osmoregulation

cards.title: What are the folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane called?
cards.body:
**Cristae**.

They greatly increase the inner membrane's surface area, which holds the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.

The space they enclose is the **matrix**; the space between the two membranes is the intermembrane space.
cards.searchQuery: mitochondria cristae inner membrane folds

cards.title: In humans, from which parent do you inherit your mitochondrial DNA?
cards.body:
Your **mother**.

The egg supplies nearly all the cytoplasm and mitochondria of the zygote, while sperm mitochondria are usually destroyed or diluted.

Example: mitochondrial DNA mutations pass from mothers to all their children.
cards.searchQuery: mitochondrial DNA maternal inheritance human

cards.title: What are the stacks of flattened thylakoid discs inside a chloroplast called?
cards.body:
**Grana** (singular: granum).

The thylakoid membranes hold chlorophyll and the light-reaction machinery. The fluid around them is the **stroma**.

Mnemonic: grana look like stacks of green coins.
cards.searchQuery: chloroplast grana thylakoid stacks

cards.title: Name the three internal compartments of a chloroplast.
cards.body:
The **intermembrane space**, the **stroma** and the **thylakoid space** (lumen).

The outer and inner membranes enclose the stroma, and the thylakoid membrane encloses a third compartment inside it.

Why: separating the thylakoid space from the stroma lets thylakoids build the proton gradient used to make ATP.
cards.searchQuery: chloroplast compartments intermembrane space stroma thylakoid lumen

cards.title: Which plastid stores starch, as in potato tubers?
cards.body:
The **amyloplast**.

Plastids are plant and algal organelles. Chloroplasts make sugar by photosynthesis; **chromoplasts** hold pigments, such as the carotenoids of ripe fruit.

Key idea: all plastids are derived from the same kind of precursor, the proplastid.
cards.searchQuery: amyloplast starch storage plastid

cards.title: Which pectin-rich layer cements the primary walls of adjacent plant cells together?
cards.body:
The **middle lamella**.

It is the first layer formed at the cell plate during cytokinesis, and a primary wall is laid down on each side of it.

Example: ripening softens fruit partly as enzymes break down pectin in this layer.
cards.searchQuery: middle lamella pectin plant cell wall

cards.title: Which polysaccharide forms strong microfibrils in the plant cell wall?
cards.body:
**Cellulose**.

Its microfibrils are embedded in a matrix of other polysaccharides and proteins.

Watch out: other walls use different polymers: fungi use chitin, and bacteria use peptidoglycan.
cards.searchQuery: cellulose microfibrils plant cell wall

cards.title: Which protein subunit polymerizes to build microtubules?
cards.body:
**Tubulin**, as $\alpha\beta$-tubulin dimers.

Dimers add to and leave the ends of a microtubule, so it can grow and shrink quickly. The end where dimers are added fastest is the plus end.

Example: at the start of mitosis, interphase microtubules disassemble and their tubulin is reused to build the spindle.
cards.searchQuery: tubulin dimers microtubule subunit alpha beta

cards.title: Toward which end of a microtubule do most kinesin motor proteins carry their cargo?
cards.body:
The **plus end**, usually pointing toward the cell periphery.

Kinesin walks along the microtubule by hydrolyzing ATP, carrying a vesicle or organelle. **Dynein** walks the opposite way, toward the minus end near the centrosome.

Mnemonic: kinesin goes out to the plus end; dynein drags toward the minus end.
cards.searchQuery: kinesin plus end microtubule motor protein direction

cards.title: In an animal cell, which structure near the nucleus is the main microtubule-organizing center?
cards.body:
The **centrosome**.

It contains a pair of centrioles surrounded by material from which microtubules grow. It duplicates before mitosis, and the two copies become the spindle poles.

Watch out: plant cells and many fungi have no centrioles but still build spindles from other organizing sites.
cards.searchQuery: centrosome microtubule organizing center animal cell

cards.title: What is the arrangement of microtubules in a centriole or in the basal body at the base of a cilium?
cards.body:
Nine **triplets** of microtubules in a ring, with no central microtubules ($9+0$).

This differs from the $9+2$ pattern of nine doublets around two central singlets in the shaft of a motile cilium or flagellum.

Key idea: basal bodies are structurally the same as centrioles, and they anchor and template the cilium.
cards.searchQuery: centriole basal body nine triplets 9+0 microtubules

cards.title: Which motor protein, attached to the doublets of a cilium, drives bending by walking between neighboring microtubules?
cards.body:
**Dynein**.

Arms of dynein use ATP to slide adjacent doublets past each other, and the protein links that hold the doublets together convert sliding into bending.

Example: in primary ciliary dyskinesia, defective dynein arms leave cilia immotile, causing chronic respiratory infections and, in men, sterility.
cards.searchQuery: dynein arms cilia flagella bending ATP

cards.title: How do cilia and eukaryotic flagella differ in number and length?
cards.body:
**Cilia** are short and numerous; **flagella** are long and few (often just one or two).

Both are extensions of the plasma membrane with a $9+2$ microtubule core, and both are anchored by a basal body.

Example: cilia sweep mucus along the human airway, while a flagellum propels a sperm cell.

Watch out: eukaryotic flagella are unrelated in structure to bacterial flagella.
cards.searchQuery: cilia versus flagella length number 9+2 eukaryotic

cards.title: Which class of cytoskeletal fibers, including keratins and lamins, is the most permanent and resists mechanical stress?
cards.body:
**Intermediate filaments**, $8\text{–}12\,\mathrm{nm}$ in diameter.

They are built from varied proteins, depending on the cell type, and form tough ropelike networks. They anchor organelles and are a main part of desmosomes.

Example: keratins strengthen skin cells and make up hair and nails.
cards.searchQuery: intermediate filaments keratin lamin cytoskeleton

cards.title: Rank the three cytoskeletal fibers from thinnest to thickest, with their approximate diameters.
cards.body:
Microfilaments ($\approx 7\,\mathrm{nm}$) < intermediate filaments ($8\text{–}12\,\mathrm{nm}$) < microtubules ($\approx 25\,\mathrm{nm}$).

Mnemonic: the names are in order of size: micro-**filament**s (smallest), **intermediate** (middle), micro-**tubules** (biggest, and hollow).

Tip: only microtubules are hollow.
cards.searchQuery: cytoskeleton fiber diameters microfilaments intermediate microtubules

cards.title: Why are phospholipids described as amphipathic?
cards.body:
Each molecule has a **hydrophilic** head (the phosphate group) and two **hydrophobic** fatty acid tails.

In water the heads face the aqueous surroundings, while the tails cluster together, away from water.

Key idea: this dual nature is why phospholipids spontaneously form membranes.
cards.searchQuery: phospholipid amphipathic hydrophilic head hydrophobic tails

cards.title: Why do phospholipids in water spontaneously assemble into a bilayer, with the tails facing inward?
cards.body:
Hiding the hydrophobic tails from water makes the system more stable.

Tails inside avoid contact with water, while heads on both faces interact with it. Bilayers close into sealed sheets or vesicles so no tails are exposed at the edges.

Why: the main driving force is the hydrophobic effect, not covalent bonding, which is why membranes can fuse and reseal.
cards.searchQuery: phospholipid bilayer self assembly hydrophobic effect

cards.title: How does cholesterol affect membrane fluidity at high and at low temperatures in animal cells?
cards.body:
It acts as a **fluidity buffer**.

At warm temperatures it restrains phospholipid movement, so the membrane is less fluid. At cool temperatures it keeps phospholipids from packing tightly, so the membrane stays fluid.

Watch out: plants lack cholesterol; they use related lipids called sterols.
cards.searchQuery: cholesterol membrane fluidity buffer temperature

cards.title: Do membranes rich in saturated fatty acids stay fluid or become more rigid at low temperature, compared with unsaturated?
cards.body:
More rigid.

Saturated tails are straight and pack tightly together. Unsaturated tails have kinks at their cis double bonds, which prevent tight packing.

Example: many organisms that live in the cold make membrane lipids with more unsaturated tails, which keeps their membranes fluid.
cards.searchQuery: saturated unsaturated fatty acids membrane fluidity kinks

cards.title: Which membrane proteins span the whole bilayer, with hydrophobic regions (often $\alpha$ helices) crossing the lipid core?
cards.body:
**Transmembrane proteins**, a kind of integral membrane protein.

Their hydrophobic segments sit among the lipid tails, and hydrophilic portions stick out into the water on one or both sides.

Example: channel proteins, carriers and many receptors are transmembrane proteins.
cards.searchQuery: transmembrane integral membrane proteins alpha helix

cards.title: What name is given to proteins that are not embedded in the lipid bilayer but loosely bound to the membrane surface?
cards.body:
**Peripheral proteins**.

They attach to exposed parts of integral proteins or to lipid heads, and many connect to the cytoskeleton or the extracellular matrix.

Key idea: they can be removed without dissolving the bilayer, unlike integral proteins.
cards.searchQuery: peripheral membrane proteins surface bound

cards.title: What carbohydrate-rich coat on the outer surface of animal cell membranes functions in cell-cell recognition?
cards.body:
The **glycocalyx**, formed by glycoproteins and glycolipids.

The sugar chains face outward, and their varied shapes act as markers that cells use to identify each other.

Example: the A and B carbohydrates on red blood cells are what define ABO blood types.
cards.searchQuery: glycocalyx glycoproteins glycolipids cell recognition

cards.title: Which kinds of molecules cross a lipid bilayer easily, and which need a transport protein?
cards.body:
**Easily**: small nonpolar molecules ($\ce{O2}$, $\ce{CO2}$, $\ce{N2}$) and small uncharged polar molecules (water, ethanol, in small amounts).

**Need a protein**: ions (e.g., $\ce{Na+}$, $\ce{H+}$), and large polar molecules such as glucose.

Why: the hydrophobic core repels anything charged or strongly polar.
cards.searchQuery: lipid bilayer permeability small nonpolar ions glucose transport

cards.title: What are the channel proteins that greatly speed the movement of water across membranes?
cards.body:
**Aquaporins**.

Water crosses a bilayer slowly by itself, but aquaporins let it flow quickly, always down its water potential gradient.

Watch out: aquaporins don't pump water; they only speed passive osmosis.
cards.searchQuery: aquaporins water channel proteins osmosis

cards.title: In osmosis, does water move toward the side of the membrane with higher or lower solute concentration?
cards.body:
**Higher** solute concentration.

Water flows across a selectively permeable membrane from the lower-solute (hypotonic) side to the higher-solute (hypertonic) side until the concentrations are equal.

Key idea: water follows its own gradient, which is the opposite of the solute's.
cards.searchQuery: osmosis water movement toward higher solute concentration

cards.title: State the water potential equation for a plant cell, and say which direction water moves.
cards.body:
$\Psi = \Psi_S + \Psi_P$, with $\Psi$ in bars or megapascals.

Water moves from **higher** to **lower** water potential. Solutes make $\Psi_S$ negative, and positive pressure (turgor) raises $\Psi_P$.

Example: pure water in an open container at standard conditions has $\Psi = 0$.
cards.searchQuery: water potential equation solute potential pressure potential plants

cards.title: State the formula for solute potential, defining each symbol.
cards.body:
$\Psi_S = -iCRT$

- $i$ is the ionization constant (1 for sucrose, 2 for NaCl)
- $C$ is the molar concentration
- $R = 0.0831\,\mathrm{L\,bar/mol\,K}$
- $T$ is the temperature in kelvin

Watch out: always convert $^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to kelvin by adding 273.
cards.searchQuery: solute potential formula iCRT water potential

cards.title: Find $\Psi_S$ in bars for a $0.1\,\mathrm{M}$ sucrose solution at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($i = 1$, $R = 0.0831\,\mathrm{L\,bar/mol\,K}$). Give the number only, to 2 decimal places.
cards.body:
$-2.48$

$\Psi_S = -iCRT = -(1)(0.1)(0.0831)(298) \approx -2.48\,\mathrm{bar}$.

Tip: the sign is always negative: dissolved solute lowers water potential.
cards.searchQuery: solute potential calculation 0.1 M sucrose 25 C bars

cards.title: A plant cell has $\Psi_S = -0.5\,\mathrm{MPa}$ and $\Psi_P = +0.3\,\mathrm{MPa}$. What is its water potential, in MPa? Give the number only.
cards.body:
$-0.2$

$\Psi = \Psi_S + \Psi_P = -0.5 + 0.3 = -0.2\,\mathrm{MPa}$.

Why: if placed in pure water ($\Psi = 0$), water would flow in because $0 > -0.2$.
cards.searchQuery: water potential calculation solute pressure potential MPa

cards.title: How do channel proteins and carrier proteins differ in the way they transport solutes?
cards.body:
**Channels** form a hydrophilic pore through which specific ions or molecules flow, very quickly.

**Carriers** bind a solute, change shape, and release it on the other side, which is slower.

Key idea: both are specific, and both can carry out passive transport; only some carriers (pumps and cotransporters) can do active transport.
cards.searchQuery: channel proteins versus carrier proteins membrane transport

cards.title: As the solute concentration outside a cell keeps rising, how does the rate of facilitated diffusion change?
cards.body:
It rises and then **levels off** at a maximum rate.

Once every carrier is busy, adding more solute does nothing: the transport proteins are **saturated**.

Why: simple diffusion has no such limit, so its rate keeps rising in proportion to the gradient.
cards.searchQuery: facilitated diffusion saturation rate plateau carriers

cards.title: What type of ion channel opens when a specific signaling molecule binds to it?
cards.body:
A **ligand-gated** (chemically gated) channel.

Binding of the ligand changes the shape of the protein, opening the pore.

Example: at a synapse, neurotransmitter binding opens ligand-gated channels on the postsynaptic cell.
cards.searchQuery: ligand-gated ion channel neurotransmitter binding

cards.title: What kind of active transport uses ATP directly to move a solute against its gradient, as the sodium-potassium pump does?
cards.body:
**Primary active transport**.

The transport protein itself is an ATPase that is phosphorylated by ATP.

Example: the $\ce{Ca^2+}$ pump of the sarcoplasmic reticulum and the $\ce{H+}$ pump of plant cells are also primary active transporters.
cards.searchQuery: primary active transport ATPase pump direct ATP use

cards.title: Intestinal cells absorb glucose by letting $\ce{Na+}$ flow in down its gradient while the same carrier pulls glucose in. What type of transport is this?
cards.body:
**Secondary active transport** (cotransport).

No ATP is used directly by the carrier. The $\ce{Na+}$ gradient it exploits was built by the $\ce{Na+}/\ce{K+}$ pump, which does use ATP.

Key idea: the energy for moving glucose uphill is stored in the sodium gradient.
cards.searchQuery: secondary active transport cotransport sodium glucose symporter

cards.title: Plants, fungi and bacteria rely on which membrane pump as the main generator of membrane potential?
cards.body:
The **proton pump** ($\ce{H+}$-ATPase).

It uses ATP to push $\ce{H+}$ out of the cell, making the inside more negative and creating a proton gradient.

Example: that gradient drives the uptake of sugars in plant cells via $\ce{H+}$-sucrose cotransport.

Why: animal cells instead use the $\ce{Na+}/\ce{K+}$ pump for this role.
cards.searchQuery: proton pump H+-ATPase plants membrane potential

cards.title: What name describes the combined driving force on an ion crossing a membrane, from its concentration difference and the membrane voltage?
cards.body:
The **electrochemical gradient**.

The chemical part comes from the concentration difference, and the electrical part from the membrane potential (the cell interior is typically negative).

Example: both forces favor $\ce{Na+}$ entering a typical animal cell, since it is more concentrated outside and the inside is negative.
cards.searchQuery: electrochemical gradient chemical electrical membrane potential ion

cards.title: What is the term for a cell engulfing a large particle or another cell with pseudopodia, enclosing it in a vacuole?
cards.body:
**Phagocytosis** ("cell eating").

The resulting food vacuole fuses with a lysosome, which digests the contents.

Example: an amoeba engulfs prey, and macrophages engulf bacteria and dead cells.

Watch out: pinocytosis ("cell drinking") takes in fluid droplets and dissolved solutes instead.
cards.searchQuery: phagocytosis engulf particle pseudopodia food vacuole

cards.title: Which animal cell junctions form a continuous seal around cells in a sheet, preventing fluid from leaking between them?
cards.body:
**Tight junctions**.

Neighboring membrane proteins fuse into a belt around the cell, so substances must pass through the cells instead of between them.

Example: they line the intestine and the bladder, keeping contents separate from the tissue beneath.
cards.searchQuery: tight junctions epithelial seal animal cells

cards.title: Which animal cell junctions act like rivets, fastening cells into strong sheets with anchoring intermediate filaments?
cards.body:
**Desmosomes**.

Intermediate filaments loop through dense plaques inside each cell, so mechanical force is spread across the whole tissue.

Example: they are abundant in skin and heart muscle, which are stretched and pulled often.
cards.searchQuery: desmosomes anchoring junction intermediate filaments skin

cards.title: What channels cross the walls of adjacent plant cells, linking their cytoplasm and plasma membranes?
cards.body:
**Plasmodesmata** (singular: plasmodesma).

Water, small solutes and even some proteins and RNAs can move through them from cell to cell.

Key idea: they are the plant counterpart of animal gap junctions.
cards.searchQuery: plasmodesmata plant cell wall channels

cards.title: Which fibrous glycoprotein is the most abundant component of the animal extracellular matrix?
cards.body:
**Collagen**.

Its strong fibers are embedded in a network of proteoglycans, giving tissues strength.

Example: collagen is the main structural protein of skin, tendon and bone.
cards.searchQuery: collagen extracellular matrix animal glycoprotein

cards.title: Which transmembrane receptor proteins bind the extracellular matrix on the outside and the cytoskeleton on the inside?
cards.body:
**Integrins**.

They relay signals from the matrix to the cell interior and let the cell transmit force to the matrix.

Example: integrin binding to the matrix helps tell a cell it is anchored; when anchorage is lost, normal cells often stop dividing.
cards.searchQuery: integrins extracellular matrix cytoskeleton receptor

cards.title: What process releases the contents of a vesicle to the outside when it fuses with the plasma membrane?
cards.body:
**Exocytosis**.

Secretory vesicles from the Golgi fuse with the plasma membrane, spilling their contents and adding membrane to the cell surface.

Example: pancreatic cells release insulin, and neurons release neurotransmitters, by exocytosis.
cards.searchQuery: exocytosis vesicle fusion plasma membrane secretion

cards.title: What is the name for endocytosis in which a cell takes in extracellular fluid and dissolved solutes in small vesicles?
cards.body:
**Pinocytosis** ("cell drinking").

The membrane dimples inward and pinches off small vesicles; it is not specific for any solute.

Watch out: phagocytosis takes in large particles, and receptor-mediated endocytosis takes in specific molecules.
cards.searchQuery: pinocytosis endocytosis fluid uptake cell drinking

cards.title: A solution with a higher solute concentration than the cell's cytoplasm is described by which term?
cards.body:
**Hypertonic**.

A cell in a hypertonic solution loses water by osmosis. Tonicity describes a solution relative to a cell and depends on solutes that cannot cross the membrane.

Mnemonic: hyper = more solute outside; hypo = less solute outside.
cards.searchQuery: hypertonic solution definition higher solute concentration than cell

cards.title: About what percent (w/v) NaCl solution is isotonic to human red blood cells?
cards.body:
About **0.9%**.

This "normal saline" has the same effective solute concentration as blood plasma, so red cells neither swell nor shrink.

Example: it is used in intravenous fluids.

Watch out: pure water given intravenously would be dangerously hypotonic and burst red cells.
cards.searchQuery: isotonic saline 0.9 percent NaCl red blood cells

cards.title: What is the term for a plant cell's plasma membrane shrinking away from the cell wall in a hypertonic solution?
cards.body:
**Plasmolysis**.

Water leaves the vacuole and cytoplasm, so the protoplast shrinks and pulls away from the wall.

Example: wilting from drought or over-fertilizing is partly due to loss of turgor.
cards.searchQuery: plasmolysis plant cell hypertonic membrane pulls from wall

cards.title: Which rigid polymer strengthens the secondary cell walls of woody plant tissues?
cards.body:
**Lignin**.

Secondary walls are laid down inside the primary wall after growth stops, and in wood and some fibers they are reinforced with lignin.

Example: lignin makes xylem vessels stiff and waterproof, so they don't collapse under water tension.
cards.searchQuery: lignin secondary cell wall wood xylem strengthening

cards.title: What is the term for the semifluid, aqueous part of the cell's interior that surrounds the organelles?
cards.body:
The **cytosol**.

The cytoplasm is broader: it includes the cytosol and the organelles (not the nucleus, in most definitions).

Watch out: the two terms are often confused. Cytosol is only the fluid; cytoplasm is the fluid plus the organelles.
cards.searchQuery: cytosol versus cytoplasm definition

cards.title: Which organelles and structures make up the eukaryotic endomembrane system?
cards.body:
The **nuclear envelope**, **ER**, **Golgi apparatus**, lysosomes, vesicles, vacuoles and the plasma membrane.

They are connected directly or by vesicle traffic.

Watch out: mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are not part of it, because they grow by importing proteins and dividing rather than receiving vesicles.
cards.searchQuery: endomembrane system components ER Golgi lysosomes vesicles

cards.title: Plasma cells, which secrete huge amounts of antibodies, are especially rich in which organelle?
cards.body:
The **rough ER** (along with the Golgi).

Antibodies are secreted proteins, which are made on ER-bound ribosomes.

Tip: cells that secrete proteins in bulk, such as pancreatic enzyme cells, show extensive rough ER; cells that make steroids show extensive smooth ER.
cards.searchQuery: plasma cells antibodies rough ER secretory proteins

cards.title: Which coat protein complex forms vesicles carrying cargo from the ER to the Golgi?
cards.body:
**COPII**.

Vesicles budding from the ER carry proteins forward to the Golgi. **COPI** vesicles carry material backward, from the Golgi to the ER, returning escaped ER proteins.

Tip: remember II for the outbound trip and I for the return trip.
cards.searchQuery: COPII vesicle coat ER to Golgi anterograde COPI retrograde

cards.title: Which family of membrane proteins helps a transport vesicle recognize and fuse with its target membrane?
cards.body:
**SNAREs**.

A v-SNARE on the vesicle pairs with a t-SNARE on the target membrane, pulling the two membranes together so they fuse.

Example: neurotransmitter release depends on SNAREs; botulinum toxin cuts them, causing paralysis.
cards.searchQuery: SNARE proteins vesicle fusion v-SNARE t-SNARE

cards.title: According to the endosymbiont theory, which organelle's origin came first, mitochondria or chloroplasts?
cards.body:
**Mitochondria**.

All eukaryotes have mitochondria or reduced versions of them, while only some (plants and algae) have chloroplasts.

Key idea: the ancestor of eukaryotes engulfed an aerobic bacterium first; the ancestor of plants and algae later engulfed a photosynthetic one.
cards.searchQuery: endosymbiont theory mitochondria first chloroplasts later

cards.title: From which group of bacteria are chloroplasts thought to have descended?
cards.body:
**Cyanobacteria**.

These are photosynthetic bacteria. Mitochondria are thought to come from an aerobic alphaproteobacterium.

Why: chloroplast DNA, ribosomes and photosynthetic machinery are most similar to those of cyanobacteria.
cards.searchQuery: chloroplast ancestor cyanobacteria endosymbiosis

cards.title: From which class of bacteria are mitochondria thought to have descended?
cards.body:
**Alphaproteobacteria**.

An aerobic alphaproteobacterium was engulfed by an ancestor of eukaryotes and became a permanent resident.

Key idea: mitochondrial DNA and ribosomes still resemble those of modern relatives of this group.
cards.searchQuery: mitochondria ancestor alphaproteobacteria endosymbiosis

cards.title: How do the membrane lipids of archaea differ chemically from those of bacteria and eukaryotes?
cards.body:
Archaeal lipids have **ether** linkages and branched hydrocarbon chains.

Bacteria and eukaryotes use **ester** linkages and unbranched fatty acids.

Example: these ether lipids help some archaea survive extreme heat and acid.
cards.searchQuery: archaea membrane lipids ether linkages branched chains

cards.title: In the classic cell-fusion experiment, mouse and human cells were fused and their surface proteins tracked with fluorescent labels. What did the result show?
cards.body:
Membrane proteins **move laterally** in the bilayer.

The two labels, initially on opposite halves of the fused cell, intermixed over time.

Key idea: this supported the fluid part of the fluid mosaic model. Proteins that are anchored to the cytoskeleton do not move this way.
cards.searchQuery: Frye Edidin cell fusion experiment membrane protein lateral movement

cards.title: What is the term for the bursting of red blood cells in a hypotonic solution?
cards.body:
**Hemolysis**.

Water enters by osmosis, and with no cell wall to resist, the cell swells until the membrane ruptures.

Watch out: lysis in general means bursting of any cell; hemolysis refers specifically to red blood cells.
cards.searchQuery: hemolysis red blood cells hypotonic bursting

cards.title: Roughly how do the typical diameters of bacterial cells and eukaryotic cells compare?
cards.body:
Bacteria: about $1\text{–}5\,\mu\mathrm{m}$. Eukaryotic cells: about $10\text{–}100\,\mu\mathrm{m}$.

Why: eukaryotic cells are larger partly because internal membranes (organelles) add surface area for exchange and compartmentalize work.

Tip: a typical eukaryotic cell is roughly 10 times wider than a typical bacterium.
cards.searchQuery: typical cell sizes bacteria eukaryotic cells micrometers

cards.title: Which family of carrier proteins moves glucose into red blood cells by facilitated diffusion?
cards.body:
The **GLUT** family (e.g., GLUT1).

GLUT carriers are uniporters that move glucose down its gradient, in either direction depending on the gradient.

Example: insulin triggers the insertion of GLUT4 into the membranes of muscle and fat cells, increasing glucose uptake.
cards.searchQuery: GLUT glucose transporter facilitated diffusion red blood cells

cards.title: What is the term for a small circular DNA molecule, separate from the main chromosome, often found in bacteria?
cards.body:
A **plasmid**.

Plasmids replicate independently and often carry extra genes, such as antibiotic resistance, that bacteria can share by conjugation.

Watch out: plasmids are not essential for normal growth, which is why they are called accessory genetic elements.
cards.searchQuery: plasmid small circular DNA bacteria resistance genes

cards.title: How does a typical bacterial chromosome differ from a eukaryotic chromosome in shape and number?
cards.body:
Bacteria usually have a **single circular** chromosome in the nucleoid. Eukaryotes have **multiple linear** chromosomes in the nucleus.

Eukaryotic DNA is wrapped around histones; bacterial DNA is supercoiled and associated with other proteins.

Watch out: some bacteria do have linear or multiple chromosomes, but a single circular one is the typical pattern.
cards.searchQuery: prokaryotic versus eukaryotic chromosome circular linear nucleoid
